title: A medieval Islamic thinker argued that fire doesn’t really burn cotton
body: In The Incoherence of the Philosophers, al-Ghazali (c. 1058–1111) took aim at thinkers who treated natural causes as necessary. Put cotton to a flame and it burns, but, he argued, nothing we observe shows that the fire *must* burn it: we only ever see one event follow another. On his view, known as **occasionalism**, God directly causes each burning, and what looks like a law of nature is God’s habit. Averroes replied a century later that God had created real natural laws; centuries on, David Hume made a similar sceptical argument about cause and effect.

left.label: The philosophers
left.text: Fire has a nature that necessarily produces burning. Cause and effect are bound together.

right.label: Al-Ghazali
right.text: We only see burning follow contact. God wills each burning directly; the fire is the occasion, not the cause.

slides.heading: The argument
items: Watch cotton touch fire: it blackens and burns
All you observed was one event, then another
Nothing you saw shows the first must produce the second
So the link is God’s habit, not a necessity

events.text: Al-Ghazali is born near Tus, in Khorasan
He becomes head of the Nizamiyya college in Baghdad
A spiritual crisis: he abandons his post and leaves Baghdad

slides.heading: Hume’s echo
slides.text: In the 18th century David Hume argued that the only place to find necessary connections is in the mind’s own associations of ideas. Al-Ghazali had reached the sceptical half of that conclusion seven centuries earlier, and drew the opposite moral: that God, not nature, does the work.

slides.heading: Earliest first
slides.explanation: Born c. 1058, the crisis of 1095, Averroes’s Incoherence of the Incoherence in the 12th century, and Hume in the 18th.
